## (Im)Pure functions in Programming

Haskell is known as a _pure_ functional programming language. We talked about
pure/impure functions previously in [this previous post about interfaces as lists of propositions](../interfaces_as_list_of_propositions/#interfaces-as-list-of-propositions).
To recapitulate: a _pure_ function is one that does not modify or depend on
_outside state_. 
Impure functions are ubiquitous, say especially in video game development:

```python
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class Player:
  x: float
  y: float
  dx: float
  dy: float

  def update(self) -> None:
    self.x += self.dx
    self.y += self.dy

def main() -> None:
  # create a new Player
  player = Player(x=0.0, y=0.0, dx=1.0, dy=1.0)
  player.update() # <- impure mutation of state "player"!
```

Haskell is notorious for not allowing such impurities:
The above can easily be rewritten by explicitly passing the required state to
the function `update`! Let's see:

```haskell
data Player = Player { x :: Float, y :: Float, dx :: Float, dy :: Float }

update :: Player -> Player
update player = player { x = x player + dx player, y = y player + dy player }

main :: IO ()
main = do
  let player = Player { x = 0.0, y = 0.0, dx = 1.0, dy = 1.0 }
  let updatedPlayer = update player
```

Here we never mutate the value of player, but instead we create a new value
`updatedPlayer` that is the result of the `update` function acting on `player`.

## Pure Categories

Pure categories are defined in “1.3.3 Pure categories” [Turaev and Virelizier, 2017, p. 14](http://link.springer.com/10.1007/978-3-319-49834-8).
Here, given a monoidal category $\mathcal{C}$, we say that $\mathcal{C}$ is 
**pure** if the left and righgt actions of 
$\text{End}_{\mathcal{C}}(\mathbf{1})$ on the sets of morphisms 
$\text{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(X, Y)$ coincide for all objects $X, Y$ of $\mathcal{C}$.
Specifically:

$$
\alpha \cdot f = f \cdot \alpha, \quad \forall \alpha \in
\text{End}_{\mathcal{C}}(\mathbf{1}), f \in \text{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(X, Y)
$$

Do you already see the connection to functional programming? No? Don't worry!
Let's dive in to what this even means.

### Monoidal Categories

A monoidal category $(\mathcal{C}, \otimes, \mathbf{1}, a, l, r)$ or simply $\mathcal{C}$
is a category $\mathcal{C}$ together with:

1. a bifunctor $\otimes : \mathcal{C} \times \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{C}$ called
   the **tensor product**,
2. a distinguished object $\mathbf{1} \in \text{Ob}(\mathcal{C})$ called the
   **unit object**,
3. a natural isomorphism $a_{X,Y,Z} : (X \otimes Y) \otimes Z \to X \otimes (Y
   \otimes Z)$ called the **associator**,
4. natural isomorphisms $l_X : \mathbf{1} \otimes X \to X$ and $r_X : X
   \otimes \mathbf{1} \to X$ called the **left** and **right unitors**,

subject to the following conditions:

- the **triangle identity**: for all objects $X, Y$ in $\mathcal{C}$, the
  following diagram commutes:
  <!-- https://q.uiver.app/#q=WzAsMyxbMCwwLCIoWCBcXG90aW1lcyBcXG1hdGhiZnsxfSlcXG90aW1lcyBZIl0sWzIsMCwiWCBcXG90aW1lcyAoXFxtYXRoYmZ7MX1cXG90aW1lcyBZKSJdLFsxLDEsIlhcXG90aW1lcyBZIl0sWzAsMSwiYV97WCxcXG1hdGhiZnsxfSxZfSJdLFswLDIsImxfWCBcXG90aW1lcyAxX1kiLDJdLFsxLDIsIjFfWCBcXG90aW1lcyByX1kiXV0= -->

- the **pentagon identity**: for all objects $X, Y, Z, W$ the following diagram
  commutes:
  <!-- https://q.uiver.app/# -->
  <iframe class="quiver-embed" src="https://q.uiver.app/#&embed" width="1092" height="432" style="border-radius: 8px; border: none;"></iframe>

This monoidal category induces a _ground monoid_
$\text{End}_{\mathcal{C}}(\mathbf{1})$ given by the endomorphisms of the unit
object $\mathbf{1}$, see decategorification[^decategorification],
and we may regard $\mathcal{C}$ as a 
vertically categorified version of this monoid[^vertically-categorified].

Now, an element $\alpha \in \text{End}_{\mathcal{C}}(\mathbf{1})$ acts on the 
sets of morphisms $\text{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(X, Y)$ as follows
$$
\alpha \cdot f := l_Y(\alpha \otimes f) l_X^{-1} \quad
f \cdot \alpha := r_Y(f \otimes \alpha) r_X^{-1}
$$

These are actions, because they satisfy the following properties for all $f \in \text{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(X, Y)$, $g \in \text{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(Y, Z)$ and $\alpha, \beta \in \text{End}_{\mathcal{C}}(\mathbf{1})$:

$$
\begin{align*}
\alpha \cdot (g \circ f) &= l_Z(\alpha \otimes (g \circ f)) l_X^{-1} \\
&= l_Z((\alpha \otimes g) \circ (\alpha \otimes f)) l_X^{-1} \\
&= l_Z(\alpha \otimes g) l_Y^{-1} \circ l_Y(\alpha \otimes f) l_X^{-1} \\ 
&= (\alpha \cdot g) \circ (\alpha \cdot f)
\end{align*}
$$

## The Connection

A _pure_ category, as stated before, is one in which the two actions 
of $\text{End}_{\mathcal{C}}(\mathbf{1})$ on $\text{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(X, Y)$
coincide. Where have we seen that before?

By the tensor-hom adjunction[^tensor-hom], we have a natural isomorphism (under the assumption that $\mathcal{C}$ is _closed_):

::: {.callout-note}
A monoidal category $\mathcal{C}$ is called **closed**[^closed] if for every object $Y$ in $\mathcal{C}$, the functor $- \otimes Y : \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{C}$ has a right adjoint (called the "internal hom"-functor[^internal-hom]), denoted by $\text{hom}(Y, -) : \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{C}$. This means that for every pair of objects $X, Z$ in $\mathcal{C}$, there is a natural isomorphism:
$$
\text{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(X \otimes Y, Z) \cong \text{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(X, \text{hom}(Y, Z))
$$
:::
